shona_text: Chikwata chevatambi venhabvu chakamira nana muzvinapembe. Ana muzvinapembe vakapfeka hembe yeyero kumusoro kuzasi vakapfeka zvikabudura zvitema.Mumwe wevatambi venhabvu kumusoro wakapfeka hembe yeruvara ruchena pamberi ine ruvara rwebhuruu neruvara ruchena. Kuzasi wakapfeka chikabudura chebhuruu kwoitawo mumwe akapfeka hembe dzeruvara rweorenji. Chikafu chakabaiwa neforogo, chinoita sechavhaidzwa chikazokangwa ndokuiswa kodzamuto  namafuta akawanda.  Chakawanda chiri mundiro uye ndokukandirwawo zvimuriwo zvakada kuita semhiripiri. Mugwagwa unofambwa nemotokari wakagadzirwa pedyo nechidziro chakareba. Chidziro ichi chinemiti irimo yakawanda, zvinoratidza kuti mune dzimba dzakawanda mukati macho. Mugwagwa  unemuti uripedyo nawo irikuoneka matanda akaoma. Uyewo hauna kana buri kana chii chinoratidza kuti mota dzinofamba zvakanaka kana dziri mumugwagwa umu. Madzimai ari munhandare maari kumhanya. Apfeka nguwo dzakasiyana dzokumhanyisa. Mudzimai ari mberi akarukwa madhiredzi ane ruvara rutema uye akamasunga nechijira chine ruvara rwebhurauni. Akapfeka nguwo yekumusoro ine ruvara rutema.
english_translation: Thing kwata chevatambi venhabvu chakamira nana in / singular zvinapembe ana in / singular zvinapembe they (past) pfeka shirt / garment yeyero to / at musoro to / at zasi they (past) pfeka things kabudura things tema.mumwe wevatambi venhabvu.

shona_text: Mugwagwa une tara nemotokari dziri kufamba, kurutivi kwacho kune mudhuri wakavakwa nemiti yakawanda Chipanera chine ruvara rwakarerekera kusirivheri , chipanera ichi chinoshandiswa kusunga nekusunungura simbi, vamwe vanosunungura simbi dzemota kana kusunga simbi dzemota, vamwe ndovanochishandisa kusunga kana kusunungura simbi dzemvura. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('mavara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'mavara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Pamusoro')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Pamusoro'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive

For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('maviri')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'maviri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). When counting 'ma-' plurals like 'maminitsi' (minutes) or 'mavara' (colours), you use 'ma-': 'madhongi maviri' (2 donkeys), 'mavara matatu' (3 colours), 'maminitsi mashanu' (5 minutes).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + Number Stem (-mwe = 1, -viri = 2, -tatu = 3, -na = 4, -shanu = 5) -> vanhu vaviri (2 people), maminitsi mashanu (5 minutes)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('kumusoro')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'kumusoro'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Mukati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Mukati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nedzimwe'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nedzimwe'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'dzimwe' forms 'nedzimwe'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('make')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'make' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('dzakasiyana')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'dzakasiyana' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('inoratidza')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'inoratidza' uses the present marker '-no-'. grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mumusoro')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mumusoro'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Mukati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Mukati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).

grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('akawaridzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'akawaridzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('anosanganisira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'anosanganisira' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('ruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'ruvara'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Highveld Weather, the Rainy Season ('Zhizha') & Farming Life

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('mukati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'mukati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakavakwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakavakwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive

For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('unoratidza')

cultural_notes.title: Highveld Weather, the Rainy Season ('Zhizha') & Farming Life

shona_text: Dzimba nhatu dzakabatana-batana.  Dzakavakwa nesamende ine ruvara rwebhurauni uyezve dzina marata ane ruvara rwesirivha uyezve panze padzo pana mahuswa mamwe akapiswa mamwe acho akaoma ane ruvara rwebhurauni. Muchina uyu unoshandiswa pamba kana mumafekitori. Unoshandiswa kubata simbi kuti dzisapfakanyika. Unobata simbi zvamandiriri. Chitoro chinotengesa zvinhu zvakasiyana siyana zvirimubhokisi. Pane kanoratidza sekunge karedhiyo kasiri mubhokokisi kane ruvara rutema. Uyezve pane tambo dzinoratidzika kuti itambo dzemagetsi dzakakura dzakawanda. Zvimwe zvirimumabhokisi hazvioneki kuti zviyi. Mudhorobha makavakwa mudhuri ichikwira mudenga. Kunewo vanhu vakawanda. Vamwe vanotengesa, vamwe varikungofamba. Panewo murume ane chikipa chine mutsetse mutsetse mutema ne orenji arikufamba, nemumwe akapfeka sheti chena ne tirauzi dema.
english_translation: Dzimba nhatu dzakabatana-batana dzakavakwa and / with samende ine colour rwebhurauni uyezve dzina plural rata ane colour rwesirivha uyezve outside on / at dzo on / at na.

grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pachikoro')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pachikoro'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Infinitive Verbs & Action Nouns with 'ku-' ('kufamba')
grammar_notes.content: Look at 'kufamba' in this sentence. Every Shona verb in its dictionary ('to do') form begins with 'ku-': for example, 'kudya' (to eat), 'kutenga' (to buy), 'kubhadhara' (to pay), 'kuona' (to see), and 'kurwa' (to fight). Because 'ku-' verbs also behave as action nouns ('eating', 'paying', 'working'), you can attach linking prefixes directly to them: 'yekubhadhara' ('for paying'), 'pakubikwa' ('in the cooking'), and 'nekuona' ('by/with seeing').
grammar_notes.rule: ku- + Verb Stem = 'to [verb] / [verb]-ing' (ku- + -tenga = kutenga, 'to buy'; ye- + kubhadhara = yekubhadhara, 'for paying')

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('egirini')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'egirini'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nepakati'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nepakati'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'pakati' forms 'nepakati'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('Chineruvara')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'Chineruvara'. grammar_notes.title: Connecting Clauses & Expressing Purpose with 'kuti'
grammar_notes.content: The connector 'kuti' is one of the most useful words in Shona. After verbs of speaking, thinking, or knowing (like 'akati' = said, 'unofunga' = you think, 'ndinoziva' = I know), 'kuti' means 'that'. However, when placed after an action verb, 'kuti' means 'so that / in order to', and the following verb changes its final vowel from '-a' to '-e'! For instance, '-dya' (eat) becomes 'kuti tidye' ('so that we may eat'), and '-wana' (get) becomes 'kuti uwane' ('so that you may get').
grammar_notes.rule: kuti + [Subject Prefix + Verb ending in -e] = 'so that [someone] may...' (e.g., kuti tidye = so that we eat)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pakati')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pakati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Joining Words with 'ne-' ('and / with') in 'nepakati'
grammar_notes.content: Look closely at 'nepakati'. In Shona, the word for 'and' or 'with' between nouns is not a separate word—instead, the prefix 'ne-' (or 'na-' before people's names) is written attached directly to the second noun! For example, 'ne-' + 'pakati' forms 'nepakati'. You will see this everywhere in daily speech: 'sadza nemuriwo' ('sadza and vegetables'), 'nesimba' ('with strength'), and 'nekukasira' ('with haste / quickly').
grammar_notes.rule: ne- + Noun = and / with [Noun] (written as a single word, e.g., sadza nemuriwo = sadza and vegetables)

Look at how location is expressed with 'pakati'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('yakagadzikwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'yakagadzikwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('pasi')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'pasi'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

grammar_notes.title: Possessive Pronouns: Saying 'My', 'Your', and 'Our' ('Shangu')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, possessive words like 'Shangu' ('my/your/our/their') always follow the noun they belong to! The six core possessive stems are '-ngu' (my), '-ko' (your), '-ke' (his/her/its), '-du' (our), '-nyu' (your plural/polite), and '-vo' (their). A short linking sound ('wa-', 'ya-', 'ra-', 'cha-', 'dza-', 'ma-') attaches to the front of the stem to match the noun: for example, 'shamwari yangu' (my friend), 'munda wako' (your field), 'mabhuku edu' (our books), and 'kubudirira kwenyu' (your success).
grammar_notes.rule: Noun + [Linking Prefix + -ngu (my) / -ko (your) / -ke (his/her) / -du (our) / -nyu (your polite) / -vo (their)]

grammar_notes.title: Counting & Numbers in Shona ('mbiri')
grammar_notes.content: In Shona, number words like 'mbiri' always come AFTER the noun they count, and their starting prefix matches the noun's group! The basic number stems are: '-mwe' (1), '-viri' (2), '-tatu' (3), '-na' (4), and '-shanu' (5). For example, when counting people ('vanhu'), you use 'va-': 'munhu mumwe' (1 person), 'vanhu vaviri' (2 people), 'varume vana' (4 men). grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('vakamira')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vakamira' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Present Tense & Everyday Actions ('vanotamba')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'vanotamba' uses the present marker '-no-'. In Shona, inserting '-no-' between the subject prefix and the verb stem expresses general truths, everyday habits, or states of mind like 'wanting', 'thinking', and 'knowing'. For example: 'ndinoda' ('I want/like'), 'unofunga' ('you think'), 'vanoti' ('they say'), and 'vanorima' ('they farm').
grammar_notes.rule: [ndi- (I) / u- (you) / a- (he/she) / ti- (we) / va- (they)] + -no- + verb -> Ndinoda (I want), Vanogara (They live)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('tsvuku')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'tsvuku'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

grammar_notes.title: Talking About Location: 'pa-', 'ku-', and 'mu-' ('Pamusika')
grammar_notes.content:
Look at how location is expressed with 'Pamusika'. Instead of separate prepositions like 'on', 'to', or 'in', Shona attaches one of three location prefixes directly to the front of a noun:
• 'pa-' means 'at' or 'on' a specific point or surface (e.g., 'patafura' = on the table, 'pamusika' = at the market, 'pasi' = on the ground).
• 'ku-' means 'to', 'from', or 'at' a general destination (e.g., 'kuchikoro' = to school, 'kumusha' = to the rural home, 'kubasa' = at/to work).
• 'mu-' means 'inside' an enclosed space (e.g., 'mumba' = inside the house, 'muguta' = in the city, 'mumugwagwa' = in the road).
grammar_notes.rule: pa- = on / at a point (patafura) | ku- = to / at a place (kuchikoro) | mu- = inside (mumba)

cultural_notes.title: Nyanga Seed Potatoes & Market Trading ('Mbatatisi Pamusika')
cultural_notes.content: Zimbabwe's cool, frost-free high altitudes in Nyanga are the country's premier region for growing potatoes ('mbatatisi'), which are sold in 15kg pockets and small heaps at urban and peri-urban markets.
